title: Channel-aware drafts: a plain-text WhatsApp welcome and a sponsor email with a subject line
prompt: Draft Kasper Olufsen's welcome message for me. My community profile is community_profile.md and the member list is members.csv. I also need a short email to Harriet Pemberton at Brindlewood Business Bank, our main sponsor, inviting her to the Founders & Operators Evening on Thursday 8 October at 6.30pm.

rubric.text: The WhatsApp welcome to Kasper is plain text: no markdown headings, no bold or italic markers, no bullet lists or tables, and no emoji in the first line.
The WhatsApp welcome is short: two to four short lines, under about 500 characters, ending in one clear question.
Both drafts end with the profile's sign-off '— Priya, Northbridge' (not '[Your name]', not 'Priya Nandakumar', not a different name).
The drafts follow the profile's voice and vocabulary: warm and brief, first names, UK spelling, no exclamation marks, people called members (never users or customers), at most one emoji.

The welcome is built around one named member for Kasper to meet, with a one-line reason drawn from members.csv and a yes/no question. It is not Ifeoma Adeyemi-Brandt (his colleague at Tidewater Robotics), and it shares no contact details.
The sponsor email has a subject line, separate from the body.

The sponsor email is formatted as an email, not as pasted WhatsApp text: a greeting by first name (Harriet), three to five short lines or one short paragraph, the event name, date and time (Thursday 8 October, 6.30pm) and a clear request to reply.
The sponsor email contains no member names or personal details; it is an invitation only and does not announce Kasper's arrival.

It does not ask the manager which channel to use for members, which for the sponsor, or what to sign off with; it takes them from community_profile.md (WhatsApp for members, email for sponsors, '— Priya, Northbridge').
Both messages are labelled as drafts for the manager to send; nothing is claimed to be sent.
